title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 01–02
description: Curated upper-intermediate vocabulary, pronunciation and word-use patterns from study skills and topic-sorting activities.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, figures, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for checked words and shorter expressions; longer expressions may omit IPA rather than supply an unreliable transcription. Pronunciation variants and connected speech are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual comparison with the teaching pages and exercise answer key; lexical/contextual review; structure and ID validation. Browser speech recognition is not tested in this environment.
audit.limitations: TTS and voice-recognition quality depend on browser, selected voice and accent; no live UI import test was performed.

units.title: Unit 01 — Learning vocabulary
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 8–9 (PDF pages 9–10).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Learn vocabulary as useful phrases and collocations, not isolated translations.
Record register, grammatical patterns and pronunciation, including stress shifts and silent letters.
Group related words by meaning and word family, and use varied authentic input.
Recognise the collocation, pronunciation and register contrasts introduced in the exercises.

items.example: The meaning changes when you add this prefix.
items.note: Meaning alone does not tell you how to use a word naturally.

items.example: She can explain the problem accurately in English.
items.note: An adverb describing correctness or precision.

items.example: Choose a phrase that fits the situation appropriately.
items.note: Suitably for a particular context or purpose.

items.example: Countability is one of a word's grammatical characteristics.
items.note: These include word class, verb patterns and countability.

items.example: Check the pronunciation before recording a new word.
items.note: The way a word is spoken, including sounds and stress.

items.example: This expression is suitable for a formal report.
items.note: Formal language fits official or serious situations.

items.example: That greeting sounds natural in an informal chat.
items.note: Informal language is typical of casual speech and writing.

items.example: A neutral word works in many different situations.
items.note: Neither especially formal nor especially informal.

items.example: Consider the register before using this term in a job interview.
items.note: A style of language associated with a situation or audience.

items.example: Learning an expression in isolation can hide its typical use.
items.note: Here it means without other words or context.

items.example: Write the whole phrase rather than a single word.
items.note: A group of words that is used together.

items.example: The phrase strong evidence is a useful collocation.
items.note: Words that are commonly used together.

items.example: Reading widely can help you develop a rich vocabulary.
items.note: Adjective + noun collocation.

items.example: My colleague listens to classical music while studying.
items.note: Use classical for the musical tradition, not classic music.

items.example: Common sense is important when assessing a risky situation.
items.note: A natural adjective + noun collocation.

items.example: Everyone had a chance to express an opinion at the meeting.
items.note: Verb + noun collocation.

items.example: I prefer not to take sides in their argument.
items.note: To support one person or group against another.

items.example: I am still in touch with former classmates.
items.note: The full fixed phrase is in touch with someone.

items.example: A good sense of humour can make teamwork easier.
items.note: British spelling: humour. Often have a sense of humour.

items.example: I was at a loss for words when I heard the news.
items.note: Describes being unable to find something to say.

items.example: I enjoy technical podcasts, in particular those about electronics.
items.note: Used to identify one especially relevant example.

items.example: Undertake is an irregular verb.
items.note: Its past forms are not formed simply by adding -ed.

items.example: Our group will undertake a new research project.
items.note: Past: undertook; past participle: undertaken.

items.example: Advice is an uncountable noun in English.
items.note: Usually not used with a/an or a plural -s.

items.example: My luggage is already at the hotel.
items.note: Uncountable: a piece of luggage, not a luggage.

items.example: These scissors are very sharp.
items.note: Plural-only form: a pair of scissors.

items.example: I memorise difficult phrases with short example sentences.
items.note: British spelling: memorise; American: memorize.

items.example: Group words according to topic or grammar.
items.note: A useful technique for organising vocabulary.

items.example: A word root can help you recognise related terms.
items.note: The basic element from which other words are formed.

items.example: She studies new words systematically each week.
items.note: In an organised, planned manner.

items.example: The dictionary is useful reference material.
items.note: Books or resources consulted for reliable information.

items.example: He reads professional literature about embedded systems.
items.note: Texts published for people working in a specialised field.

items.example: A weekly podcast provides useful listening practice.
items.note: An online audio programme or episode.

items.example: The speaker explained a common regional expression.
items.note: A person who grew up speaking a language as a first language.

items.example: Mouse has an irregular plural: mice.
items.note: A plural formed in an unusual way.

items.example: The two proposals have a subtle difference.
items.note: The letter b is silent.

items.example: Losing the entire dataset would be a catastrophe.
items.note: The final -e is pronounced as a syllable.

items.example: She teaches chemistry at university.
items.note: The letters ch represent a /k/ sound.

items.example: Could you answer this question in English?
items.note: The w is silent in the standard pronunciation.

items.example: The lab keeps a record of every test.
items.note: As a noun, the stress is on the first syllable.

items.example: We need to record the results before shutting down.
items.note: As a verb, the stress is on the second syllable.

items.example: The report contains a photograph of the test rig.
items.note: Stress falls on the first syllable.

items.example: The photographer arrived before the event.
items.note: Stress moves to the second syllable.

items.example: We need photographic evidence of the installation.
items.note: Primary stress falls on the third syllable.

items.example: The team made remarkable progress.
items.note: Common collocation: remarkable progress or remarkable difference.

items.example: Researchers sometimes coin new words for discoveries.
items.note: Here coin means invent or create an expression.

items.example: The royal family attended the ceremony.
items.note: Other natural combinations include royal palace and royal welcome.

items.example: There is a subtle difference between the two designs.
items.note: Subtle commonly combines with difference, shade or suggestion.

items.example: Are you guys ready for the presentation?
items.note: Informal address for a group; usage varies by context and audience.

items.example: The venue has additional rules for a minor.
items.note: A relatively formal or legal term for someone under the legal age.

items.example: That is an awesome result!
items.note: Informal praise; prefer more measured wording in formal reports.

items.example: Passengers should alight at the next station.
items.note: Formal word for getting off a bus or train.

items.example: I felt gutted when our experiment failed.
items.note: British informal expression meaning extremely disappointed.

items.example: The report described the suspect as a convicted felon.
items.note: A legal term, particularly common in the United States.

items.example: Please tell me if these messages bug you.
items.note: Informal verb meaning annoy or bother someone.

items.example: I sometimes zone out during long meetings.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for becoming inattentive.

items.example: She can articulate a complicated technical argument.
items.note: Formal verb for expressing ideas clearly.

items.example: The chart conveys the main finding clearly.
items.note: To communicate an idea, message or feeling.

items.example: He put across his idea with a simple diagram.
items.note: Phrasal verb: communicate an idea successfully.

items.example: I used a screwdriver to tighten the terminal.
items.note: A hand tool used to turn screws.

items.example: Water began to drip from the damaged pipe.
items.note: A verb for liquid falling in small drops.

items.example: The article covers a remarkable range of subjects.
items.note: Remarkable is used to emphasise an unusually impressive amount or variety.

items.example: The two brothers have a remarkable likeness.
items.note: A likeness is a resemblance between people or things.

items.example: It was a remarkable coincidence that we met abroad.
items.note: Coincidence refers to events happening together unexpectedly.

items.example: The journalist helped coin a phrase that became popular.
items.note: Coin as a verb means create a new term or expression.

items.example: Scientists may coin a term to name a new concept.
items.note: Similar pattern to coin a phrase.

items.example: Visitors toured the royal palace.
items.note: Royal describes things associated with a king or queen.

items.example: The guests received a royal welcome at the hotel.
items.note: Often figurative: a very warm or impressive welcome.

items.example: She made a subtle suggestion during the discussion.
items.note: Subtle can describe indirect or not immediately obvious meaning.

items.example: The two words express different subtle shades of meaning.
items.note: Shade can refer to a small difference in meaning or colour.

items.example: The poem describes a kingly figure.
items.note: An adjective derived from king; often literary.

items.example: The actor entered with a regal manner.
items.note: A formal adjective meaning fit for a king or queen.

items.example: A shadowy figure appeared in the doorway.
items.note: Related to shadow; also means unclear or mysterious.

sectionsChecked: A: What do you need to learn?
B: What does knowing a new word mean?
C: How can you help yourself to memorise words?
D: How can you help yourself learn more words?

units.title: Unit 02 — Organising a vocabulary notebook
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 10–11 (PDF pages 11–12).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Organise words with meaning networks, word-class categories and related word families.
Record frequent word partners, fixed expressions, synonyms and antonyms.
Notice stress changes between noun and verb forms.
Practise topic sorting and meaningful contrasts using vocabulary from the exercises.

items.example: My vocabulary notebook is divided into useful topics.
items.note: Store related words, examples and grammar notes together.

items.example: I organise technical terms by subject.
items.note: British spelling: organise. American: organize.

items.example: Create a broad section for feelings and emotions.
items.note: A general rather than very narrow category.

items.example: Make a chart of verbs and related nouns.
items.note: A visual way of arranging or presenting information.

items.example: The piano is a musical instrument.
items.note: A tool for producing music; also used for scientific devices.

items.example: She prefers classical music to pop music.
items.note: Classical music is not usually called classic music.

items.example: The festival included traditional folk music.
items.note: Music associated with a community's traditions.

items.pt: música do mundo; músicas de diferentes tradições
items.example: The station has a programme devoted to world music.
items.note: A broad industry label for music from different cultural traditions.

items.example: She began to strum her guitar.
items.note: Typically strum a guitar or another string instrument.

items.example: The group will perform at the concert tonight.
items.note: Perform can also mean carry out a task or procedure.

items.example: The final track on the album is instrumental.
items.note: A recorded piece of music on an album.

items.example: The band will release an album next month.
items.note: Release can mean make music, software or other products publicly available.

items.example: Regular practice improves pronunciation.
items.note: In British English, practice is the noun.

items.example: I practise speaking English three times a week.
items.note: In British English, practise is generally the verb.

items.example: A network diagram links related expressions.
items.note: A visual map of concepts and their relationships.

items.example: She uses a social network to share professional news.
items.note: A social platform or a network of connected people.

items.example: You need to sign up before using the platform.
items.note: Often sign up for a service or course.

items.pt: remover alguém dos amigos (em rede social)
items.example: He decided to unfriend an inactive contact.
items.note: Remove someone from a social-network friends list.

items.pt: publicação no X (antigo Twitter); publicar no Twitter
items.example: She posted a tweet about the conference.
items.note: Term used for posts on Twitter, renamed X; legacy terminology in the 2017 book.

items.example: A virus can damage files on an unprotected computer.
items.note: Also means a biological infectious agent.

items.example: Use a unique password for each account.
items.note: A secret combination used to access an account.

items.example: Identity theft can lead to fraudulent transactions.
items.note: Criminal misuse of someone else's identity details.

items.pt: enviar arquivo para a rede; fazer upload
items.example: Please upload the report before midday.
items.note: Transfer a file from your device to a remote service.

items.example: Download the dataset before the training session.
items.note: Transfer a file from a remote service to your device.

items.example: I will post the announcement on the team page.
items.note: Verb or noun in online communication.

items.example: Send me the link to the documentation.
items.note: Can mean a web address or a connection between things.

items.example: I sometimes surf the web to find language resources.
items.note: An informal expression for browsing websites.

items.example: A pop-up interrupted the page.
items.note: A window or message that appears automatically.

items.example: The documentation is linked from the homepage.
items.note: The main starting page of a website.

items.example: Could you forward the message to our manager?
items.note: When used for email, forward means send a received message on.

items.example: The confirmation email went to junk mail.
items.note: Unwanted messages, often advertising.

items.example: The filter blocked several spam messages.
items.note: Unsolicited or bulk electronic messages.

items.example: Keep the whole collocation in your notes.
items.note: Words that commonly occur together.

items.example: Our colleague managed to win a prize for her research.
items.note: Use win with prize, award or medal.

items.example: Engineers can earn a salary while studying part-time.
items.note: Earn commonly combines with money, salary and income.

items.example: Extra preparation helped us gain an advantage.
items.note: Gain can combine with time, experience or an advantage.

items.example: Learn a fixed phrase as a whole.
items.note: A group of words normally used together in a set form.

items.example: I was in a hurry and forgot my notebook.
items.note: Use in a hurry, not on a hurry.

items.example: I have been out of touch with former classmates.
items.note: May mean no longer in contact or unaware of developments.

items.pt: de um lado para o outro
items.example: The cable moved to and fro in the wind.
items.note: Describes repeated movement in opposite directions.

items.example: We review our old notes now and again.
items.note: Synonym of occasionally.

items.example: Glad is a synonym of pleased in many contexts.
items.note: Words with the same or similar meanings.

items.example: Urban and rural are antonyms in this exercise.
items.note: Words with opposite meanings.

items.example: Public transport is widely used in urban areas.
items.note: Opposite in this context: rural.

items.example: The company operates in a rural region.
items.note: Opposite in this context: urban.

items.example: The equipment will cease operating during maintenance.
items.note: A formal alternative to stop.

items.example: Decide which word class fits the sentence.
items.note: For example: noun, verb, adjective or adverb.

items.example: Produce and productive belong to the same word family.
items.note: Related words built from a shared base.

items.example: The factory can produce several components per hour.
items.note: Verb; stressed on the second syllable.

items.example: The market sells locally grown produce.
items.note: Noun meaning farm-grown food; stress on the first syllable.

items.example: The new product passed all the tests.
items.note: Related to produce and productive.

items.example: We had a productive discussion this morning.
items.note: Related adjective in the produce family.

items.example: Word stress changes between the two uses of produce.
items.note: A syllable made more prominent than others.

items.example: Continuous stress can affect concentration.
items.note: May refer to emotional pressure or phonetic emphasis.

items.example: She took a rest after a week of exhaustion.
items.note: Extreme physical or mental tiredness.

items.example: Overwork can reduce productivity.
items.note: Too much work; can be a noun or verb.

items.example: He felt burnt out after several stressful months.
items.note: Exhausted after sustained pressure; British spelling burnt.

items.example: I am snowed under with work this week.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning extremely busy.

items.example: The engineering team is under pressure to finish testing.
items.note: Often be under pressure to do something.

items.pt: passar tempo com alguém; sair com alguém
items.example: I like to hang out with friends at weekends.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for spending leisure time together.

items.example: She is a casual acquaintance rather than a close friend.
items.note: Someone you know but do not know very well.

items.example: I am close to my former university friends.
items.note: Describes a strong personal relationship.

items.example: You can count on her when you need help.
items.note: To rely on or trust someone.

items.example: A tabloid published a short article about the event.
items.note: A newspaper style often associated with popular stories.

items.example: The announcement spread through the blogosphere.
items.note: Collective name for blogs and their online community.

items.example: A journalist interviewed the project manager.
items.note: A person who reports news.

items.example: She writes a blog about science.
items.note: A regularly updated website or online publication.

items.pt: enviar um vídeo para a internet
items.example: We plan to upload a video of the demonstration.
items.note: A common verb + object combination.

items.example: The latecomer missed the introduction.
items.note: A person arriving later than expected.

items.example: My alarm clock rings at seven.
items.note: Device used to wake someone at a set time.

items.example: Set an alarm so you do not oversleep.
items.note: The book uses set a clock; set an alarm is a more precise everyday collocation.

items.example: I had a nightmare before the exam.
items.note: An unpleasant or frightening dream.

items.example: Do not rush through the safety checks.
items.note: Can be a verb or noun.

items.example: I overslept and missed the early train.
items.note: Past: overslept. Means sleeping later than intended.

items.example: She had to dash to the station.
items.note: Here dash is a verb meaning hurry or run.

items.example: I started to yawn during the late lecture.
items.note: Can be a noun or verb.

items.example: He was breathless after climbing the stairs.
items.note: Adjective describing difficulty breathing normally.

items.example: She was exhausted after working all night.
items.note: Stronger than tired.

items.example: Deep sleep is important for recovery.
items.note: A natural adjective + noun collocation.

items.example: The children were fast asleep by ten.
items.note: Fixed combination: fast asleep, not quickly asleep.

items.example: As a heavy sleeper, he rarely hears the alarm.
items.note: A person who is not easily woken.

items.example: I was out of breath when I reached the platform.
items.note: Fixed phrase describing breathlessness.

items.example: The client was pleased with the prototype.
items.note: Often followed by with or to + infinitive.

items.example: I am glad you enjoyed the demonstration.
items.note: Similar to pleased in many contexts.

items.example: The photographer took a great shot of the bridge.
items.note: Informal synonym for a photograph in this context.

items.example: They were dissatisfied with the service.
items.note: Opposite of satisfied.

items.example: Long shifts may deprive workers of enough sleep.
items.note: Pattern: deprive someone of something.

items.example: I prefer spicy food to mild dishes.
items.note: Opposite of mild when describing food.

items.example: It is a chilly morning, so take a jacket.
items.note: Slightly or unpleasantly cold.

items.example: The design team aimed for perfection.
items.note: Noun related to perfect and perfectionist.

items.example: The team is trying to perfect the design.
items.note: Verb: stress on the second syllable.

items.example: A perfectionist may spend extra time on small details.
items.note: Person who wants everything to be perfect.

items.example: Please inform the team about the schedule change.
items.note: Often inform someone about or of something.

items.example: This information is important for the experiment.
items.note: Uncountable: some information, not an information.

items.example: The seminar was clear and informative.
items.note: Provides useful information.

items.example: She is interested in politics and public policy.
items.note: A noun referring to activities or ideas of government.

items.example: The debate has political consequences.
items.note: Adjective related to politics.

items.example: The politician spoke about education.
items.note: A person professionally involved in politics.

items.example: He decided to study economics at university.
items.note: Academic discipline that studies resources and economic activity.

items.example: We need to economise on materials.
items.note: British spelling: economise; often economise on something.

items.example: The policy has important economic effects.
items.note: Relates to the economy, not necessarily to saving money.

items.example: This engine is economical to run.
items.note: Means not wasteful or inexpensive to use.

items.example: An economist analysed the report.
items.note: A specialist in economics.

items.example: I need to set the clock to the correct time.
items.note: The exercise uses set a clock. Set an alarm instead when you mean choose a wake-up time.
